clue.text: Small, and weighing little?

parts.note: S is the size printed on a clothing label, the standard short form for small
anything that weighs little is light

explanation.surface: A thing small enough and light enough to pick up without noticing.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate definition to hunt for: the sentence describes the answer and spells it out at the same time. The question mark is the setter admitting the whole line has to be read twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Slight means small in size or amount, and a slight build is a light one, so the sentence read straight is the word itself.

clue.text: Hot under the collar — like certain clothes?

definitions.note: The second definition is the setter's invention rather than a dictionary sense: the ending -y turns a noun into 'resembling that thing', and the question mark owns up to it.
definitions.meaning: the state of a person whose temper has gone and whose neck has got warm with it
read as a garment plus the -y that means 'of that kind', it describes what one particular item of clothing is like

explanation.surface: Someone losing their temper, with a glance at what they have got on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot under the collar' is an idiom about temper and a remark about a shirt in the same six words, which is why the two halves sit so comfortably together. The second reading has no dictionary behind it at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirty is British for bad-tempered — 'don't get shirty with me' — and the same letters read as a garment with the ending that means 'like one'.

clue.text: Unbeliever I find condemned to the bowels of hell!

indicators.note: A condemned building is one marked for demolition, and letters treated that way come down and go back up in another order.

parts.note: five letters rearranged

indicators.note: The bowels of a place are deep inside it, so only the inner letters of the word named are wanted.

parts.note: the two letters at the heart of HELL, once its outsides are stripped off

explanation.surface: A damned unbeliever being sent down to the deepest part of hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Condemned' means damned on the surface and broken up in the parse, and it is doing both jobs in one word. The exclamation mark covers hell being used as raw spelling rather than as a place.
explanation.definitionFit: An infidel is someone outside the faith in question — the word the Crusades used for the other side — so 'unbeliever' is the plain synonym.

clue.text: Some Finnish or Norwegian instrument

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so what is wanted is a run of the letters standing there rather than the words themselves.

parts.note: the run starts on the last letter of Finnish, takes the whole of 'or' and stops at the first letter of Norwegian

explanation.surface: A musical instrument that comes from somewhere in Scandinavia.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nationalities side by side look like a choice being offered, and the little joining word between them is carrying half the letters. That is where hidden answers like to sit: the eye never stops on 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: A horn is a brass instrument sounded by blowing — the French horn, the horn section — so the bare word names it by its family.

clue.text: Hop season

definitions.meaning: a short jump off the ground
the one between winter and summer, when everything starts growing again

explanation.surface: The part of the year when the hops are ready.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, nothing in between to mark the join. 'Hop' is the verb, not the plant that the pairing with a season puts in your head.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring is to leap off the ground, which is what hopping is; and spring is the season that follows winter.

clue.text: Fish cheek served up with vegetable

indicators.note: Up is backwards in a down answer, so the word this points at is written from the foot of the column towards the top.

parts.note: cheek in the sense of impudence is lip, here turned round
chard is the leaf beet sold as greens

explanation.surface: A fish course coming to the table with vegetables beside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' is impudence rather than the side of a face, and 'served up' belongs to the kitchen on the surface while it turns a word round in the parse. The pilchard is the grown-up sardine, the mainstay of the old Cornish fishery.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilchard is a full-grown sardine, an oily sea fish sold tinned in tomato sauce, so 'fish' names it by its kind.

clue.text: Expression I love written in grey

parts.note: the clue's own letter, taken exactly as it stands

indicators.note: Writing something in puts it inside what is already on the page, so this letter goes into the middle of the word named next.

parts.note: a dim light is a grey one, weak and drained of colour
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a nought

explanation.surface: A phrase about love set down in grey ink.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter that starts the clue is doing nothing but being itself, which is the hardest sort of piece to notice. The tennis nought goes inside the word for dull light rather than beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a set phrase whose sense is not the sum of its words, like 'kick the bucket', and expression is the everyday word for one.

clue.text: Laugh in concert with endless delight

indicators.note: An endless word has lost its end, so the final letter of the one that follows never gets used.

parts.note: a gig is a booked live performance
delight is glee, with the last letter taken off

explanation.surface: People laughing together at a show they are thoroughly enjoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In concert with' reads as the idiom for doing something jointly, and it is hiding the musician's word for a booking. Glee is delight in the older sense, which survives in glee club and gleeful.
explanation.definitionFit: To giggle is to laugh in a light, breathy, half-suppressed way, so the bare verb 'laugh' is the plain synonym.

clue.text: Recent union member, sweet thing and dreamer

parts.note: the sweet stuff out of the hive, and what you call someone you are fond of
to moon is to drift about in a daydream, so one who does it is a mooner

explanation.surface: A new trade unionist who is sweet-natured and inclined to daydream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' is marriage rather than the trade sort, and 'member' is one of the two people in it. Mooning about is the old sense of the verb, nothing to do with dropping your trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeymooner is one of a couple away on the holiday that follows the wedding, so they belong to a union entered into very recently.

clue.text: Blaze, ground on fire, engulfing mountain finally

indicators.note: To engulf a thing is to swallow it whole, so the letters doing it close around the one named next.
Ground is what a mill does to grain, breaking it up completely, so these letters are not left as they stand.

parts.note: six letters rearranged

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word in front of it, and only that last letter is taken.

parts.note: the letter standing at the end of MOUNTAIN

explanation.surface: A news bulletin: fire running across open ground and taking the mountain at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' reads as the land the fire is crossing and works as the past tense of grind. Definition and fodder are both about fire, which is how the setter keeps one hidden inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is a large, fierce, out-of-control fire, and blaze is the newspaper word for the same thing.

clue.text: Slippery on the ground?

definitions.note: The second definition gives a position rather than a synonym — something on the ground is lying there — and the question mark marks the stretch.
definitions.meaning: the shifty sense: a slippery witness is not to be believed
stretched out flat, the way anything dropped on the floor ends up

explanation.surface: A warning that the ground underfoot is treacherous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery' invites ice and means untrustworthy. The answer's two senses come from two different verbs that happen to share every letter: to lie, to tell an untruth, and to lie, to be stretched out.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody slippery cannot be trusted with the truth, which is what lying means; and anything on the ground is lying there, from the other verb to lie.

clue.text: Kerfuffle — still incomplete?

definitions.note: The second definition describes a job rather than naming one: what is still incomplete is still to do, and the question mark flags the shift from noun to phrase.
definitions.meaning: a fuss, a commotion, a great deal of noise made about something
the state of a job nobody has got round to, the line left unticked on the list

explanation.surface: A fuss that has not yet blown over.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the only join between the two halves: one is a noun for a commotion, the other the phrase at the head of every list of jobs. The British 'to-do' for a fuss comes from the older 'much to do'.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is British for a fuss or uproar — 'what a to-do' — and a task still to do is one nobody has finished.

clue.text: Meat scoffed by celeb after stirring sauce

indicators.note: To scoff food is to eat it up, so whatever does the scoffing closes right round the word in front of it.
What comes out after stirring is not arranged as it went in, so those letters are used in a new order.

parts.note: five letters rearranged
ham is the cured meat off the pig's hind leg

explanation.surface: A celebrity wolfing down a plate of meat once the sauce has been stirred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' sits at the end of the line, where a solver expects the fodder to be heading, and it is the definition. Béchamel is the white sauce of butter, flour and milk that lasagne and cauliflower cheese are built on.
explanation.definitionFit: Béchamel is one of the French mother sauces, milk thickened with a butter-and-flour roux, so 'sauce' names it by its kind.

clue.text: Silly old prig, a wastrel

indicators.note: A silly arrangement is not a sensible one, so the letters that follow are not standing in the order they ought to be.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters, the comma counting for nothing

explanation.surface: Calling somebody a foolish, prudish old waster.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything but the last word is fodder, and the comma is there only to make the insult scan. The prodigal son of the parable ran through his inheritance, which is where the spendthrift sense comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A prodigal is someone who spends recklessly and has nothing left to show for it, which is exactly what a wastrel is.

clue.text: Blue material almost runs out

indicators.note: Almost a word is not quite all of it, so the last letter of the one that follows never arrives.
Something out is out of its proper place, so the letters this acts on are not used in the order printed.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
runs gives up its last letter, adding three more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: The dye running out of a blue cloth in the wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue material' looks like one phrase and splits straight down the middle, the first word defining and the second supplying letters. Ultramarine was ground from lapis lazuli shipped from beyond the sea, which is what its Latin name says.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultramarine is a deep, vivid blue pigment, so the bare colour word names it by the shade it is.

clue.text: Zip broken in thong

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart, and the pieces can be put back together in any order at all.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: The zip on a scrap of skimpy underwear has given way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zip' is the slang nought, not the fastener the thong puts in your head, and 'broken' does damage to clothing on the surface while rearranging letters underneath. The little word 'in' is fodder, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is slang for zero — 'we got zip out of him' — and nothing is the plain word for that same absence.

clue.text: Pin down basic resource

definitions.meaning: fasten sheets of paper together with a little bent wire so they cannot move
the commodity a country or a diet is built on, like rice, wheat or wool

explanation.surface: Pinning down which resource a place cannot manage without.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves are a verb and a noun with nothing to mark where one ends and the other begins. The commodity sense comes from the medieval staple, the town granted the monopoly on selling a particular good.
explanation.definitionFit: To staple sheets is to pin them down with a wire fastener, and a staple is the basic commodity a place lives on — wheat, rice, oil.

clue.text: Push New and Old Testament in conclusion

indicators.note: New means made over into something that was not there before, so the letters in front are rebuilt rather than kept as they are.

parts.note: four letters rearranged
OT is the standard short form for the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A preacher finishing up by pushing both Testaments at the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New and Old Testament' reads as a matched pair, and only the second half of it supplies letters — the first word is the instruction. An upshot was originally the final shot of an archery match, which is where the sense of outcome comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The upshot of something is how it turns out in the end, which is what a conclusion is.

clue.text: Port road renewed means of access

indicators.note: Renewing a thing makes it over out of the same material, so these letters are reused in a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Roadworks have resurfaced the route down to the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port road' looks like a description of somewhere and is eight letters of fodder. The definition is kept vague on purpose: this is a way in, but a way in through a floor, a ceiling or a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapdoor is a hinged panel set into a floor, ceiling or stage that opens to let you through, so it is a means of access.

clue.text: A bloom developed

parts.note: the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands
the rose is the bloom every garden has

explanation.surface: A flower coming along nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'a' is doing nothing but being a letter, which is the oldest trap in a short clue. 'Developed' is past tense, so the answer has to be past tense too — a problem developed, a problem arose.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that arose came up or came about, which is what 'developed' says of a situation or a difficulty.

clue.text: Pull the plug on vessels when turned round

indicators.note: Turning a thing round leaves it facing the other way, so those letters are read from the back.

parts.note: pots are vessels for cooking or for plants, here written backwards

explanation.surface: Emptying the sink of the pans that have been stood upside down in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull the plug on' means putting an end to something, and the sink the idiom came from is exactly where the vessels are placed to keep you. Pots are the crossword's standard vessels, along with urns and ewers.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull the plug on a project is to stop it, so the idiom and the plain verb both name bringing a thing to a halt.

clue.text: Faint, wiping brow — it's fever!

indicators.note: To wipe something away is to take it off altogether, so the letter named goes and the rest closes up.

parts.note: a faint memory or a faint outline is a vague one
the brow sits at the top of a face, so it points at the letter at the top of that word — in a down answer, the first

explanation.surface: Someone light-headed mops their forehead, and it turns out to be fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint' is the adjective for indistinct, not the swoon the surface is arranging. Ague is the old name for malarial fever, the kind that comes with fits of shivering, and it long outlived its use in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: An ague is a fever marked by shivering and sweats — the malarial sort that used to haunt English marshland — so 'fever' names it by what it does.

clue.text: Spike's beginning to relish getting into funk

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its first letter, so that single letter is all this takes from what follows.

parts.note: funk is British slang for a bad smell, and so is pong

indicators.note: Getting into a thing means going inside it, so this letter is planted in the middle of the word named next.

parts.note: the first letter of relish, taken because the clue asks only for its beginning

explanation.surface: Spike is starting to enjoy getting into funk music.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is simply 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay, and the capital letter makes the first word look like somebody's name. Funk is a stink in British slang long before it is a kind of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A prong is one of the points of a fork or an antler, so 'spike' names it by the sharp projection it is.

clue.text: Single failing with hard language

indicators.note: A failing thing is coming apart, and letters that come apart are free to be put back in another order.

parts.note: six letters rearranged
H is the grade stamped on a hard pencil

explanation.surface: Somebody on their own is failing a difficult subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard' is the pencil grade, the H beside the B on the side of every pencil. The last word of a clue is where a solver expects more fodder, and here it is the definition instead.
explanation.definitionFit: English is a language, so the definition names the class the answer belongs to rather than offering a synonym for it — definition by example, which crosswords allow.

clue.text: The same throughout, though lovely on the outside

parts.note: both words give ground in the same way: 'lovely even so' and 'lovely though it is' concede the same point

indicators.note: What is on the outside of a word is its first and last letters, so the middle of the one named is left behind.

parts.note: the first and last letters of LOVELY

explanation.surface: Something the same all the way through and beautiful on the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the outside' looks like part of the compliment the surface is paying and is an instruction to strip a word down to its ends. The definition is an adverb: spread at one rate the whole way through.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something evenly is to do it at the same rate all the way through, so the adverb and the phrase say one thing.

clue.text: Maximum number on end of branch

indicators.note: In an across answer one thing written on another comes after it, so the piece named first is the one that ends up behind.
The end of a word is its last letter, and that single letter is all this takes.

parts.note: the letter standing at the end of BRANCH
the number 8, spelt out in letters

explanation.surface: The greatest number of something to be found out at the tip of a branch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maximum' is the noun — the height of fashion, the height of summer — rather than the adjective the surface is offering. 'Number' names no particular one, so which number is wanted is settled by the rest of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The height of something is its topmost point or its extreme degree, as in the height of luxury, which is what a maximum is.
